translations.translatedText: # Tuesday 2.1.2018 (radio)

There are at least a million people in Finland who find it hard to handle things electronically. Finns are worried about climate change. A new method has been introduced in Finland for treating tumours. Food is being transported to Lapland for tourists from different countries.
## A million Finns have fallen off the digital sled
![computer and paper receipts](https://img.img-cdn.yle.fi/crop_fill,w_767,h_431,dpr_1/f_auto/13-3-9990851)
Open image viewer
Photo: Chameleons Eye / AOP
There are at least a million people in Finland who find it hard to handle things electronically.

In addition to older people, many young people are also in this group. In Finland there are 250 000 excluded young adults who suffer from language problems. There are just as many who have some physical obstacle or disability. Statistics Finland says that about half a million people over 65 do not use the internet.

Health and youth do not always help. For example, a child may have a mobile phone with which it is possible to buy a ticket for a local train. Without an online bank account or credit account, however, they cannot buy a ticket.
A researcher estimates that the problems of digital exclusion will trouble people for decades.
## Finns are worried about climate change
![Infographic](https://img.img-cdn.yle.fi/crop_fill,w_767,h_431,dpr_1/f_auto/13-3-10000364)
Open image viewer
Photo: Taloustutkimus, Harri Vähäkangas / Yle
Finns are more and more worried about climate change. About 90 percent say that climate change is a very serious or fairly serious problem.
The worry is affected, among other things, by Finns' high level of education and trust in science. In addition, Finns' relationship with nature is strong.
Finns' worry about the climate has grown as the economic crisis has begun to ease.
## A new treatment for tumours
![Physicist Teija Sainio at the HIFU device.](https://img.img-cdn.yle.fi/crop_fill,w_767,h_431,dpr_1/f_auto/13-3-9992480)
Open image viewer
Physicist Teija Sainio presents the HIFU device. Photo: Minna Rosvall / Yle
A new method for treating tumours has been introduced in Finland. The method is called HIFU.

In it, tumours are treated with ultrasound, without surgery or radiotherapy. In the treatment, the patient lies on top of the HIFU device and is pushed into an MRI scanner. In HIFU treatment, the energy of the ultrasound is transferred to the tumour. When the temperature rises high enough, the tissue dies and the tumour gradually goes away.

Finland's only HIFU device is at Turku University Hospital. About 40 patients have been treated there. In the future, the brain, among other things, may be treated. Worldwide there are more than 200 HIFU devices. About 20 000 treatments have been carried out with them.
Ultrasound treatment does not replace radiotherapy, but both treatments can be used at the same time.
## Food is transported north to tourists
![Food being taken from the buffet line onto a plate.](https://img.img-cdn.yle.fi/crop_fill,w_767,h_431,dpr_1/f_auto/13-3-9770776)
Open image viewer
Photo: Wasim Khuzam / Yle
Tourism in Lapland shows up in food transport on the roads. The different food cultures of tourists have increased food transport on the northern roads.
Wholesale transport has increased by a third in the last few years. For example, British people must be offered British food, and Asian people food they know.

In Lapland many people are puzzled by tourists who travel to an exotic place but want to eat only food from their own culture. Tour operators set the menu and also try to keep the price reasonable with it.
